Peromyscus maniculatus neonates emerge into the world at a remarkably modest body mass, with field-collected data indicating newborn pups weigh approximately 2 grams [Wwb = approximately 2 grams]. This altricial birth mass is typical for small-bodied cricetid rodents and reflects the relatively short gestation period of 24 days [tg = 24 days] measured under standard captive conditions at a body temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. During this roughly three-week gestational window, the developing embryo undergoes rapid organogenesis and achieves sufficient somatic differentiation to support a live birth, yet the offspring remain highly underdeveloped. The low neonatal mass places considerable energetic demands on the lactating female, who must provision her litter intensively to sustain the swift growth trajectory that characterizes the pre-weaning phase. Comparative data from other Peromyscus species suggest this birth weight is near the lower boundary for the genus, although intraspecific variation linked to maternal nutrition and litter size has been documented across the species' broad geographic range.

Weaning represents a critical developmental milestone in the life history of the eastern deer mouse, marking the transition to nutritional independence. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], pups achieve weaning at 22 days after birth [tx = 22 days after birth], at which point they typically attain a wet weight of 9.2 grams [Wwx = 9.2 grams]. This tripling of birth mass from 2 grams [Wwb = 2 grams] over a period of just over three weeks underscores the exceptionally high growth rate facilitated by the mother's milk, which is rich in lipids and proteins relative to many other rodent species. The timing of weaning coincides closely with the developmental maturation of the digestive system, allowing the juvenile to process solid food items such as seeds and insects. Field studies have revealed some geographic variation, with populations from colder, more seasonal environments occasionally exhibiting a slightly protracted nursing period, presumably to build greater fat reserves before facing independent foraging challenges.

Sexual maturity in female Peromyscus maniculatus is attained relatively early in life, facilitating the species' capacity for rapid population turnover. Under the standard thermal conditions of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], females reach puberty at 49 days since birth [tp = 49 days since birth], a point at which the reproductive tract becomes fully functional and the first ovulation may occur. This rapid maturation, occurring less than two months after birth, is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction in response to high rates of extrinsic mortality. The adult body mass continues to increase through the early breeding months, ultimately reaching a plateau at approximately 20.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 20.5 grams]. This ultimate wet weight represents the asymptotic size achieved after somatic growth ceases, though males and females may show slight differences in mean adult mass depending on local ecological conditions.

The reproductive output of Peromyscus maniculatus is characterized by moderate litter sizes and a high potential for iteroparity across the breeding season. Females typically produce litters of 5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 5 pups per litter], and under the favorable environmental conditions maintained at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C], they achieve on average approximately 3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 3 litters per year]. This combination of litter size and reproductive frequency yields a substantial annual reproductive output that allows populations to rebound quickly following periods of low density. The brevity of the 24-day gestation (24 days) [tg = 24 days] is characteristic of small cricetids and enables the rapid serial litters that underpin the species' high reproductive potential during resource-rich seasons at a temperature of 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C]. Postpartum estrus is common in this species, meaning that a female may become pregnant again within hours of giving birth, further compressing the interbirth interval and maximizing lifetime fecundity in environments where resources are abundant.

Longevity in the eastern deer mouse is comparatively modest, reflecting the species' position as a small, short-lived mammal subject to significant predation pressure. The maximum lifespan recorded in captive colonies maintained at 36.6 °C [T = 36.6 °C] is approximately 8.3 years [am = approximately 8.3 years], substantially exceeding that of most murid rodents of comparable size and attributed to the evolutionarily conservative metabolic strategy of Peromyscus species under conditions of high extrinsic mortality. Field-based estimates are typically much lower due to environmental hazards. The species exhibits a pattern of gradual senescence, with reproductive decline becoming noticeable after the second year of life in most individuals. In natural populations, few animals survive beyond a single breeding season, making the captive longevity estimate a useful benchmark for understanding the species' intrinsic physiological limits. Comparative gerontological studies have noted that Peromyscus species generally outlive laboratory mice of the genus Mus, a difference attributed to their evolutionary history in variable, predation-rich environments.
